# GitHub Workflows Design (v2.19)

This document describes the GitHub Actions workflow architecture for the `three` monorepo.

> **Scope constraint:** Each project maps to exactly one language ecosystem. Multi-language projects (e.g., a C# library with a companion npm package) are out of scope and must be split into separate project directories with separate `release.json` files.

> **Release-unit constraint:** Each `buddy.yml` or `official.yml` run releases exactly one project. Coordinated multi-project release orchestration is out of scope for this design.

## 1. Architecture Overview (Shared Execution Layer)

To avoid duplicating build and deploy logic across the primary validation and release entry workflows, the design adopts a shared execution layer made of reusable workflows plus reviewed local composite actions. Each entry workflow independently invokes the checked-in execution paths it needs — there is no single dispatching hub.

**Entry layer (Entry Workflows):** `ci.yml`, `buddy.yml`, `official.yml`

**Execution layer (Reusable Workflows under `.github/workflows/`):**

- `_build-test-csharp.yml` — runs on `windows-latest`
- `_build-test-python.yml` — runs on `ubuntu-latest`
- `_build-test-jsts.yml` — runs on `ubuntu-latest`
- `_build-test-ruby.yml` — runs on `ubuntu-latest`
- `_attest-build-csharp.yml` — runs on `ubuntu-latest`
- `_attest-build-python.yml` — runs on `ubuntu-latest`
- `_attest-build-jsts.yml` — runs on `ubuntu-latest`
- `_attest-build-ruby.yml` — runs on `ubuntu-latest`
- `_publish-nuget.yml` — publishes `.nupkg` to the GitHub Packages NuGet feed for buddy runs
- `_publish-npm.yml` — publishes npm tarballs to the GitHub Packages npm registry for buddy runs
- `_publish-rubygems.yml` — publishes gems to the GitHub Packages RubyGems-compatible host for buddy runs

The split axis is still **ecosystem (tooling)**, not destination, but there are now two explicit direct-job exceptions. The first is official publication. GitHub OIDC binds external trust to the workflow identity that actually mints the token, and the public provider contracts reviewed for March 2026 document GitHub Actions trusted publishing for `npmjs`, `PyPI`, `RubyGems.org`, and `NuGet.org`, but they still differ in selector fields, login helpers, runtime prerequisites, and documented unsupported compositions. In particular, reviewed npm docs validate the calling workflow name when `workflow_call` is involved, PyPI still treats reusable workflows as unsupported trusted-publisher workflows, and RubyGems publicly documents reusable-workflow support. This design therefore standardizes every official external publish job (`nuget:official`, `npm:official`, `pypi:official`, and `rubygems:official`) plus the official GitHub Release publish job (`github:official`) as direct jobs in `official.yml`, not because every provider exposes the same selector contract, but because one reviewed direct caller path per release channel removes provider-specific ambiguity from the repository control plane. The second exception is `buddy.yml`'s direct `pypi:testpypi` job, because the reviewed `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish` action keeps its trusted-publishing step in a top-level workflow job even for TestPyPI. Reviewed local composite actions or helper scripts may still encapsulate step sequences inside those direct jobs when the upstream contract supports that shape, because they execute under the same entry-workflow job identity after the job-level environment and permission gates are established. What is forbidden is reusable-workflow indirection or any other separate workflow hop for official publication, and for PyPI-family trusted publishing the actual `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish` step itself must remain direct. Each publish job still mutates **exactly one** destination. `nuget:official` and `rubygems:official` each remain one logical official target even though `official.yml` implements each as exactly one of two mutually exclusive direct jobs selected from the frozen auth mechanism; those splits model two credential paths to the same destination, not two destinations. For `npm:official`, the locked toolchain used by the production path must also satisfy Node `>= 22.14.0` and npm CLI `>= 11.5.1`; this is a design prerequisite, not an implementation detail, and must be asserted from reviewed toolchain state before the job becomes publish-eligible. For `npm:official`, this design also treats npm's automatically generated native provenance for eligible trusted-publishing runs as a parallel provider-native evidence chain, but eligibility is narrower than "trusted publishing was used": npm's reviewed docs require a public package and a public source repository, and private repositories remain explicitly ineligible even when the package itself is public. The authoritative same-run repository-visibility fact for that decision must be emitted once by `resolve-context` as `repository-visibility` with the closed set `{public, private}`, derived from GitHub's runtime repository metadata for the current run, and every later npm-native-provenance check in this workflow must consume that emitted value rather than re-deriving visibility from drift-prone post-publish reads. The direct publish job must therefore not add a redundant manual `--provenance` path, must emit `npm-native-provenance-classification`, and must classify the run as exactly one of `{expected, intentionally-disabled, not-applicable-private-repository, not-applicable-private-package, not-applicable-private-repository-and-package}` before `confirm-publish-state` consumes that result as supplemental evidence rather than as a replacement for the GitHub attestation gate. That closed set now has one explicit operator-controlled intent path: `npm-native-provenance-intent` with values `auto | disabled`. `intentionally-disabled` is legal only when that intent is `disabled` **and** the run would otherwise be npm-native-provenance-eligible (`repository-visibility = public` plus public package access). Package access must be derived in one reviewed precedence chain: npm registry metadata `access` first, the packed tarball's `publishConfig.access` second, validated `release.json` `npmAccessHint` third, then the explicit fallback `unscoped => public`; an exact-package metadata `404` before a first publish counts as "metadata absent, continue to the next reviewed source" rather than as a hard failure. Only after all of those reviewed signals are absent does a scoped package become indeterminate and hard-fail instead of being silently treated as `not-applicable-private-package`. That package-access resolution is a pre-publish gate, not a post-publish discovery path: `resolve-context` must validate the checked-in hint early for `npm:official`, `publish-npm-official` must resolve the effective access before the first registry mutation, must emit that exact fact as `resolved-package-access`, and must pass an explicit `--access` whenever checked-in policy is the deciding signal. `confirm-publish-state` must consume `resolved-package-access` plus `resolve-context.outputs.repository-visibility` as the authoritative same-run gating facts for npm-native-provenance validation instead of recomputing those truths from possibly drifted post-publish read paths. An `intentionally-disabled` result is a controlled discrepancy, not a log-only footnote: if the run later reaches a terminal success path with that classification, `release-complete` must trigger the reviewed recovery-ledger update path so `.github/release-recovery-ledger.jsonl` receives one `audit` record with `scope = "single-release-identity"`, `result = "discrepancy-found"`, `evidenceUrl` pointing to the workflow run URL, and `nextReviewAt` no later than 7 days after the run. In normal operation that reviewed recovery-ledger update path is PR-only rather than a direct push to `main`: the originating run must emit a machine-readable candidate ledger payload, and `.github/workflows/official-run-health-monitor.yml` on `refs/heads/main` is the reviewed automation that may open or refresh the corresponding minimal ledger-update PR. Direct ledger pushes remain reserved for the documented break-glass path only. For `rubygems:official`, `providerContractStatus = audience-undocumented` is not sufficient by itself: the preferred path remains trusted publishing, but the frozen inventory may also select one reviewed fallback `authMechanism = api-key-secret` that uses a scoped RubyGems.org push key through the protected environment variable `RUBYGEMS_FALLBACK_API_KEY`, consumed only as `GEM_HOST_API_KEY` by the publish step. To keep least privilege symmetric with NuGet, official RubyGems publication must therefore split into `publish-rubygems-official-trusted-publisher`, which carries `id-token: write` and is eligible only when `authMechanism = trusted-publisher`, and `publish-rubygems-official-api-key`, which carries only `contents: read` and is eligible only when `authMechanism = api-key-secret`. When the frozen inventory selects `trusted-publisher`, official RubyGems publication must also be guarded by a non-mutating trusted-publisher credential-exchange canary plus a fail-closed readiness snapshot gate before human approval is consumed. The unresolved `audience-undocumented` contract gap is intentionally bounded rather than indefinitely renewable: renewal counts `0` and `1` remain ordinary reviewed renewals, renewal count `2` already requires written sign-off from the security committee or organizational security leadership as a merge prerequisite plus an `audit` ledger record with `scope = "control-plane-monitoring-governance"`, `evidenceUrl` pointing to the sign-off or reviewed governance issue/PR, and `nextReviewAt` no later than 30 days after merge, and renewal count `3` is the absolute ceiling. A PR may land that third renewal only when it also records the concrete transition plan to either adopt the published audience contract, switch `rubygems:official` to `authMechanism = api-key-secret`, or fail-close/remove the target; no fourth renewal is legal in this design. When the inventory instead selects `api-key-secret`, the same protected environment-scoped fallback remains mutually exclusive with OIDC selector fields, the api-key direct job must never request an OIDC token, and the path is entered only through the reviewed recovery flow.

For `official.yml`, the protected control-plane branch set is the default branch `main` plus eligible protected maintenance branches `release/<project-name>/v<release-line>`, where `<release-line>` is the numeric release line such as `1.2.x` without a leading `v`. The branch selected in the `workflow_dispatch` UI, or the branch ref supplied through the REST API, supplies both the trusted workflow/control-plane code and the release payload source for that run. Tag refs and every other non-branch ref are unsupported in this design and must hard-fail before checkout. Official release tags are derived and created by the workflow itself from the selected protected source ref after validation succeeds; they are not external workflow inputs.

Trusted control-plane **code** follows the same rule with one stricter exception for privileged monitoring reads. For `official.yml`, the caller workflow, every reusable workflow, every composite action, and every helper script that performs privileged release gating or publishing come from the same dispatch-selected protected source branch once the run leaves `preflight-check`. The checked-in control-plane **state** is separate: `.github/official-caller-refs.json`, `.github/official-dispatch-authorizers.json`, `.github/publish-trust-inventory.json`, `.github/provenance-signer-map.json`, and `.github/release-recovery-ledger.jsonl` are authoritative only on `refs/heads/main`. Official runs must therefore freeze one control-plane snapshot from `main` in `authorize-dispatcher`, pass that immutable SHA into `preflight-check`, re-emit it unchanged from `preflight-check`, and use that same snapshot consistently for branch eligibility, dispatcher authorization, trust-inventory validation, signer-map validation, and any helper code executed while project-scoped preflight monitoring credentials are live. Recovery-ledger schema validation is enforced in CI when the ledger changes; official-time behavior instead consumes the reviewed recovery helpers and runbook semantics defined later in this design. During `preflight-check`, the dispatch-selected protected source branch is treated as data-only input rather than as a trusted source of helper code.

**Secrets:**

- **Build-test workflows** have no secret requirements. Callers must pass `secrets: {}` and must not pass any non-empty `secrets:` map. This blocks caller secret forwarding and limits the blast radius if a compromised dependency or malicious test reads the environment during build/test execution. It does **not** disable the job `GITHUB_TOKEN`; that token is controlled only by `permissions`.
- **Reusable publish workflows** must also be called with `secrets: {}` and must not receive any non-empty `secrets:` map. Direct official publish jobs are ordinary jobs rather than reusable-workflow calls, so they do not declare a job-level `secrets:` map; instead they rely on job `permissions`, OIDC, and environment-scoped credentials. Blanket `secrets: inherit` is prohibited in this design.

Permissions are inherited automatically: a reusable workflow receives the caller job's `permissions` grants as long as the reusable workflow itself does **not** declare its own `permissions` block. This is what allows the same `_publish-nuget.yml` to operate under `packages: write` when called from `buddy.yml`, while all official publication happens directly in `official.yml` and buddy publish workflows stay reusable.

> **Important constraint:** Reusable workflows must NOT declare their own `permissions:` block. If they do, only the scopes explicitly declared there remain eligible, and each of those scopes is still capped by the caller job's grant. Undeclared scopes become `none` even if the caller granted them. For example, if a reusable workflow declares `permissions: { id-token: write }` and the caller grants only `packages: write`, the minted token will have both `id-token: none` and `packages: none`, causing silent runtime failures. Keep all `permissions:` declarations in the entry workflows only.
>
> This rule must be lint-enforced in repository policy. In addition to `actionlint`, the repository must run a custom `hk` validation that matches `^\.github/workflows/_.*\.yml$` and fails if any such reusable workflow declares either a workflow-level or job-level `permissions:` block. This rule has no exceptions in this design.


> **Important constraint:** Shell input hardening applies to both entry workflows and reusable workflows. No `run:` step may interpolate `${{ inputs.* }}`, `${{ github.event.inputs.* }}`, `${{ github.* }}`, `${{ needs.*.outputs.* }}`, `${{ env.* }}` values derived from those contexts, or any other untrusted expression directly into shell source. In practice, shell source must not contain `${{ ... }}` expansions for untrusted values at all. All such values must first be mapped under `env:` and then referenced only as quoted shell variables such as `"$PROJECT_NAME"`.

> **Important constraint:** Mapping untrusted values through `env:` is necessary but not sufficient. Shell steps must also ban `eval`, `bash -c`, PowerShell `Invoke-Expression`, and other dynamic command construction with untrusted data; must pass any untrusted positional value after an explicit `--` end-of-options separator when the target CLI supports one; must write `GITHUB_ENV`, `GITHUB_OUTPUT`, `GITHUB_PATH`, and `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` only through helpers that reject embedded newlines and delimiter injection; must not derive here-doc delimiters or workflow-command file syntax from untrusted values; must not enable shell tracing around credential-handling steps; and must not print untrusted values to stdout or stderr in legacy workflow-command form. Repository policy must lint these sinks in addition to checking for direct `${{ ... }}` interpolation in `run:` blocks. Where Bash is used in trusted shell steps, the workflow or composite action must declare `shell: bash` explicitly so the reviewed hardening contract is not left to runner defaults. The allowed workflow-command-file writers are not implicit: `hk.pkl` must define an explicit reviewed allowlist of helper entrypoints, and any direct command-file write outside that allowlist is a hard failure. Those helper entrypoints must live only under trusted control-plane paths already covered by `CODEOWNERS` and the `infra` inventory. `confirm-publish-state` adds one stricter special case: `hk.pkl` must also statically identify every helper entrypoint that may run as a parallel confirmation worker and hard-fail any **direct** write from those helpers to `GITHUB_OUTPUT`, `GITHUB_ENV`, or `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`. This design does not require `hk.pkl` to prove the full transitive subprocess write closure statically; transitive containment instead comes from `CODEOWNERS` review on the worker entrypoints plus the mandatory launcher behavior that unsets `GITHUB_OUTPUT`, `GITHUB_ENV`, and `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` before each worker `exec`. Worker communication is scratch-directory-only in this design.

> **Important constraint:** The same shell-hardening rule also applies to local composite actions under `.github/actions/**`. Any value received through a composite action's `with:` inputs is still untrusted at the point where that composite action consumes it. Composite-action `run:` steps must therefore map those values through `env:` before use, must avoid direct `${{ inputs.* }}` interpolation in shell source, and must be covered by the same repository-policy linting for unsafe workflow-command-file writes and dynamic shell execution.

**Protected environments:** Official releases use one protected GitHub environment per mutable destination, two dedicated write environments, one project-scoped non-human-gated preflight monitoring environment, and one repository-scoped governance-monitoring environment. The publish environments are `production-nuget-<project-name>`, `production-npm-<project-name>`, `production-pypi-<project-name>`, `production-rubygems-<project-name>`, and `production-github-<project-name>`. Each official publish job must enter only its own exact target environment; sharing one environment across multiple trusted-publisher jobs is unsupported because it would collapse the provider-facing trust boundary and let one compromised job mint OIDC tokens for unrelated audiences. `production-tag-write-<project-name>` is a separate tag-reservation environment used only by `create-release-tag`; it carries the release-tag writer App private key and must never be referenced by registry, provenance, or GitHub Release publish jobs. `production-evidence-write-<project-name>` is a separate evidence-persistence environment used only by `require-provenance`; it carries the release-evidence writer App private key and must never be referenced by registry, GitHub Release, or tag-reservation jobs. `control-plane-monitoring-<project-name>` is a project-scoped environment used only by `official.yml` `preflight-check` for that exact project; it carries the environment-reader and ruleset-auditor App credentials for that project's preflight reads and exists specifically so maintenance-branch onboarding or retirement for one project cannot pause official publication for unrelated projects. `control-plane-governance-monitoring` is a repository-scoped environment used only by the allowlisted monitoring workflows that need audit credentials, the dedicated organization-scoped audit-log monitor App credential used by governance monitoring, and outbound monitor secrets. The ruleset-auditor App remains operationally read-only for this design, but GitHub's current Rulesets API requires the minimum write-level ruleset permission to read `bypass_actors`, so that credential must be isolated there explicitly.

The target-specific publish environments plus the tag-write and evidence-write environments must each use the same exact deployment branch set for the project, the same required-reviewer protection profile, and no environment wait timer. `control-plane-monitoring-<project-name>` is intentionally different: it must have **no** required reviewers and no wait timer, because GitHub Environments block all jobs that reference an environment until one configured reviewer approves them, and `preflight-check` must run before any production approval is consumed. Its deployment branch set must equal only that selected project's exact protected control-plane refs from `main`, not the repository-wide union. `control-plane-governance-monitoring` is also intentionally non-human-gated and must have **no** required reviewers and no wait timer, but unlike the project-scoped preflight environment it is entered only by schedule-driven or `workflow_run`-driven monitors from `main`; its deployment branch policy therefore remains `main`-only. Both monitoring environment classes must instead rely on exact deployment-branch policy, zero registry credentials, and repository policy that limits which workflows may reference them. Intentional release holds are operational decisions outside the workflow, not durable checked-in exception state, so approval-latency monitoring in this design measures only human review latency. GitHub Environments still treat required reviewers as a one-of-N approval pool rather than a dual-approval gate, so the at-least-two-reviewer requirement in this design is reviewer-pool redundancy, not a claim that GitHub will require two approvals. Every protected environment in this design must also define an environment-scoped variable `CONTROL_PLANE_ENVIRONMENT_ROLE` whose exact value identifies its intended role: `monitoring-preflight`, `monitoring-governance`, `tag-write`, `evidence-write`, `publish-nuget`, `publish-npm`, `publish-pypi`, `publish-pypi-testpypi`, `publish-rubygems`, or `publish-github`. `publish-pypi-testpypi` is reserved for the dedicated buddy TestPyPI environment and is intentionally outside the official production-environment family. Every environment-gated job must verify the expected value before any GitHub App token mint, OIDC request, or external mutation. This is a mandatory fail-closed guard against GitHub's documented behavior of auto-creating a referenced missing environment without protection rules or secrets. It is intentionally narrower than a full live environment-integrity proof: a wrong or missing value catches deleted-and-auto-recreated environments and obvious miswiring, but an already-existing protected environment can still drift in ways that preserve a syntactically valid role string, so `preflight-check`'s live environment validation and the control-plane drift monitor remain authoritative.

**Permissions model:** Every entry workflow declares `permissions: {}` at workflow level. Individual jobs then request only the scopes they need (principle of least privilege). Key scopes:

| Job kind                                         | Required `permissions` |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- |
| Read repository metadata / releases              | `contents: read`       |
| Enumerate workflows, workflow runs, and repository Actions metadata | `actions: read` |
| Read pull request file lists                     | `pull-requests: read`  |
| Read-only checkout and trusted helper code       | `contents: read`       |
| Push protected official release tags             | `contents: read` on the job `GITHUB_TOKEN`; the actual protected-tag write uses a dedicated GitHub App installation token |
| Create or update official GitHub Releases        | `contents: write`, `actions: read` |
| Publish to GitHub Packages                       | `packages: write`      |
| Generate official attestations in the isolated language-matching attestation job | `contents: read`, `id-token: write`, `attestations: write` |
| Verify build attestations and persist durable evidence in `require-provenance` | `contents: read`, `actions: read` |
| Trusted-publisher publish to supported official registries | `contents: read`, `actions: read`, `id-token: write` |
| Official publish via reviewed `api-key-secret` fallback | `contents: read`, `actions: read` |

For jobs that mutate GitHub Releases, `contents: write` is the actual write-capability floor exposed by GitHub. The extra `actions: read` shown in this design is not a Releases-API primitive; it is required only because the same jobs must rerun the synchronous same-project admission recheck immediately before mutation.

Official registry auth is intentionally split by documented provider capability. `npmjs` and `PyPI` use their documented trusted-publisher flows directly in `official.yml`. `NuGet.org` prefers GitHub Actions trusted publishing through `NuGet/login@v1` or a reviewed successor that mints a short-lived API key inside the approved environment, and in that preferred mode the approved `production-nuget-<project-name>` environment must provide `NUGET_USER` as an environment-scoped variable so the direct official publish path can satisfy the action's required `user` input. Because `NuGet/login@v1` returns that short-lived credential as the step output `NUGET_API_KEY`, this design reserves the distinct name `NUGET_FALLBACK_API_KEY` for the mutually exclusive long-lived fallback environment secret. The trusted-publisher path must consume only `steps.<login-step-id>.outputs.NUGET_API_KEY` and must immediately remap it to a non-conflicting local variable such as `NUGET_OIDC_API_KEY` before `dotnet nuget push`; reading ambient `NUGET_FALLBACK_API_KEY` on the trusted-publisher path is malformed because it can accidentally bind the wrong credential source. However, `NuGet/login@v1` is still comparatively young upstream infrastructure, so `nuget:official` must also support one explicitly reviewed, mutually exclusive fallback auth mode recorded in `.github/publish-trust-inventory.json`: `authMechanism = api-key-secret`, where the same protected environment carries a long-lived `NUGET_FALLBACK_API_KEY` secret and the direct job publishes with `dotnet nuget push --api-key` instead of using `NuGet/login@v1`. To preserve least privilege while still allowing the synchronous pre-mutation admission recheck, `official.yml` must split NuGet publication into two mutually exclusive direct jobs selected from the frozen inventory: `publish-nuget-official-trusted-publisher` declares `permissions: { contents: read, actions: read, id-token: write }` and is eligible only when `authMechanism = trusted-publisher`, while `publish-nuget-official-api-key` declares `permissions: { contents: read, actions: read }` and is eligible only when `authMechanism = api-key-secret`. Both jobs use the same target-specific protected environment, the same reviewed helper action, the same recovery identity, and the same `confirm-publish-state` / `release-complete` logical target mapping for `nuget:official`; exactly one of them may run in any single official attempt, and the non-selected job must remain `result == "skipped"`. When `authMechanism = trusted-publisher`, `NUGET_FALLBACK_API_KEY` must be absent; when `authMechanism = api-key-secret`, `NUGET_USER`, `trustedPublisherSelector`, and NuGet OIDC audience fields must be absent. Switching between those two NuGet modes is a reviewed control-plane change and must update the trust inventory in the same PR. The trigger set for that switch is closed and mutually classified rather than overlapping by accident: use criterion (1) when a formal upstream or provider incident, advisory, or deprecation notice exists; use criterion (3) only when the same condition is reproducible internally **without** such a formal upstream notice. For this policy, one reviewed `failure signature` means the same failing path (`NuGet/login@v1` itself or the immediately surrounding OIDC token-exchange call), the same normalized provider or HTTP error class or reviewed error-string family, and the same GitHub-hosted image family. The counted evidence must span at least two distinct official run attempts that were otherwise publish-eligible after reviewed validation of local inputs such as `NUGET_USER`, selected package identity, and caller-ref eligibility. To avoid treating one broken project configuration as a repository-wide platform event, the preferred evidence still spans at least two distinct projects or two distinct protected caller refs whenever the repository contains them; when the repository currently exposes only one `nuget:official` project or only one eligible protected caller ref for that project, two otherwise publish-eligible failures for that same project/ref may satisfy the repository-wide floor. At least one of the following reviewed evidence predicates must be satisfied and recorded in the same control-plane change set before the fallback-flip PR is merge-eligible: (1) an upstream or provider incident, advisory, or deprecation notice that directly affects `NuGet/login@v1` or its token-exchange path; (2) a reviewed evidence package showing at least two consecutive or three rolling repository-wide trusted-publisher failures across any `nuget:official` run within 24 hours on GitHub-hosted runners where the failing step is the OIDC exchange or `NuGet/login@v1` path rather than package-content validation, the evidence shows each counted run would otherwise be publish-eligible, and the counted failures share the same reviewed failure signature rather than project-local misconfiguration such as a wrong or missing `NUGET_USER`; (3) a reviewed reproducible compatibility regression between `NuGet/login@v1` and the current GitHub-hosted image or GitHub OIDC contract when no formal upstream or provider notice exists for that same condition; (4) a reviewed rollback from a prior temporary fallback enablement after the trusted-publisher path has been revalidated by at least one complete successful `nuget:official` trusted-publisher run that reaches `confirm-publish-state.outputs.confirmation-state = complete`; or (5) a written directive from the organization's security committee or audit function, accompanied by an independent reviewed security assessment recorded in the same change set. Those criteria define the minimum reviewed evidence for landing the control-plane PR that flips `authMechanism`; they do not auto-switch runtime behavior, and the authoritative mechanism remains a human-led reviewed PR plus the recovery/runbook flow in Section 7. Criterion (2) is intentionally repository-wide in this monorepo because a genuine OIDC or `NuGet/login@v1` platform incident will affect every `nuget:official` project path, while project-specific credential-shape or package-validation errors must be excluded from that count. Every `nuget:official` target must also keep one pre-staged reviewed fallback activation path materialized as a reproducible control-plane snapshot whose only semantic effect is the fallback flip plus its coupled credential-shape assertions. That snapshot may be a dedicated branch or another reviewed repository-resident minimal change set, but it must remain reproducible from trusted control-plane state without reconstructing the change ad hoc during an incident. Governance monitoring must validate that snapshot at least every 7 days by running the same CI gates that would apply to the real fallback change and by recording a readiness snapshot that includes the validated source SHA, validation timestamp, and result in the recovery ledger or a linked tracked issue. This design intentionally does **not** require a permanently open or permanently pre-approved PR for the fallback path. When an actual fallback enable or disable is needed, release engineering must open a fresh PR from the latest validated snapshot, or an equivalent regenerated minimal change set with the same semantics, and complete the normal branch-protection and `CODEOWNERS` approval flow before merge. Every fallback enable or disable change must record its evidence URL, `credentialId` when applicable, and a `nextReviewAt` no more than 7 days later in the recovery ledger or a linked control-plane audit issue. `rubygems:official` follows the same reviewed auth-mechanism model as `nuget:official` and therefore must also split into two mutually exclusive direct jobs selected from the frozen inventory. Its preferred path is trusted publishing and retains `providerContractStatus = audience-undocumented` while RubyGems public docs omit a fixed audience literal. The reviewed fallback is `authMechanism = api-key-secret`, where the same protected environment carries `RUBYGEMS_FALLBACK_API_KEY` and the direct helper exposes it only as `GEM_HOST_API_KEY` for `gem push`. To preserve least privilege while still allowing the synchronous pre-mutation admission recheck, `publish-rubygems-official-trusted-publisher` must declare `permissions: { contents: read, actions: read, id-token: write }` and is eligible only when `authMechanism = trusted-publisher`, while `publish-rubygems-official-api-key` must declare `permissions: { contents: read, actions: read }` and is eligible only when `authMechanism = api-key-secret`. Both jobs use the same target-specific protected environment, the same reviewed helper action, the same recovery identity, and the same logical-target mapping for `rubygems:official`; exactly one of them may run in any single official attempt, and the non-selected job must remain `result == "skipped"`. When `authMechanism = trusted-publisher`, `RUBYGEMS_FALLBACK_API_KEY` must be absent and the trusted-publisher selector plus provider-contract-status fields must be present. When `authMechanism = api-key-secret`, those OIDC selector and audience fields must be absent, the fallback key must be a scoped push-only RubyGems.org key, and the api-key direct job must skip any OIDC request entirely. Repository-side trust inventory plus the exact environment or selector mapping remain the project-specific control-plane proof, while registry-level readiness snapshots are only provider-path health signals; a healthy snapshot must never be described as proof that the selected project's external trusted-publisher selector is already wired correctly. This design now requires early-readiness signals for every production target that depends on trusted-publisher health. `NuGet.org` and `RubyGems.org` use non-mutating trusted-publisher credential-exchange checks against their real production providers rather than scheduled package-publish canaries; the routine monitor stops once the provider accepts the GitHub OIDC identity and returns the expected short-lived publishing credential, and it must not push synthetic production versions on a 30-minute cadence. `pypi:official` consumes a TestPyPI trusted-publisher canary that exercises the same PyPI-family OIDC flow against the reviewed pre-production endpoint, and `npm:official` consumes a dedicated public npmjs canary package path that proves the same GitHub-hosted trusted-publisher contract on npmjs. These readiness signals are admission gates for the matching production targets, not claims that any sandbox and production endpoints are identical; stale or failed snapshots always fail closed, but their recorded failure class must distinguish provider outage from monitor-execution delay. npmjs may auto-generate provenance for eligible public packages when trusted publishing is used, but reviewed npm docs make that ineligible for private repositories even when the package itself is public; this design therefore requires `publish-npm-official` to classify whether npm-native provenance is `expected`, `intentionally-disabled`, `not-applicable-private-repository`, `not-applicable-private-package`, or `not-applicable-private-repository-and-package`, and to carry that classification into `confirm-publish-state` and durable evidence as a supplemental chain. GPR feeds use `GITHUB_TOKEN` with `packages: write` instead.

Because GitHub attestations are bound to the job that generates them, this design isolates attestation generation into a dedicated language-matching attestation job that performs no dependency installation, package restore, or test execution. The release-mode build job therefore runs without OIDC, produces only the manifest-selected artifacts plus deterministic verification inputs, and uploads them as immutable workflow artifacts. The attestation job downloads that artifact set, validates it, mints the OIDC-backed attestation bundles, and uploads a provenance sidecar artifact. `require-provenance` then downloads both artifacts, verifies the bundles against the expected attestation-job identity, and writes the durable evidence record. `require-provenance` must not mint a second attestation set for already-built artifacts.

GitHub Releases management does not expose a narrower `releases: write` permission in GitHub Actions. `contents: write` is therefore the minimum available scope for the direct `publish-github-official` job in this design.

That `contents: write` grant is repository-scoped rather than project-scoped. The target-specific `production-github-<project-name>` environments in this design provide approval and review isolation, not a separate GitHub Release permission namespace.

The GitHub App installation tokens used by `create-release-tag` and `require-provenance` are repository-scoped rather than ref-scoped. Ref-level isolation for `refs/tags/release/**` and `refs/heads/release-evidence` therefore comes from repository rulesets plus the dedicated protected environments, not from a narrower App permission shape.

Because GitHub's write credentials are repository-scoped primitives in this design, project-scoped environments must not be described or treated as independent write namespaces. A job that starts with `contents: write`, or that later mints a repository-scoped GitHub App write token, has repository-wide write capability for the full lifetime of that credential; a later composite-action boundary or a "single helper step" convention does not narrow that scope. The design therefore minimizes such jobs structurally rather than pretending the permission is step-local: after the required environment-role check and read-only checkout are complete, the job may execute only the one reviewed target mutation path plus the mandatory immediate post-mutation re-read / bounded rollback logic for that same target, and it must not run any additional checkout-sourced code, arbitrary shell expansion, or unrelated mutation path while the credential remains live.

> **Note:** With `permissions: {}` at workflow level, jobs that run `actions/checkout` or read GitHub release metadata must explicitly declare at least `permissions: { contents: read }`. In this design, `preflight-check`, build jobs, gate jobs, and any other job that performs a read-only checkout must therefore request `contents: read`. Any job that performs the synchronous same-project admission recheck against workflow runs or immutable artifacts — namely `preflight-check`, `require-provenance`, `create-release-tag`, and the direct official publish jobs — must additionally request `actions: read`, because that recheck enumerates `official.yml` runs and reads repository Actions-scoped metadata. GitHub environment and ruleset metadata are still read through the dedicated audit App installation tokens rather than through the job `GITHUB_TOKEN`, because GitHub Actions does not document an `environments` workflow-permission key and the ruleset-auditor contract remains App-based.

**Repository protection model:** This design uses GitHub repository rulesets for protected branches and protected tags. Legacy branch-protection endpoints and compatibility shims are out of scope before implementation starts. Workflow preflight and policy validation query the Environments API plus the Repository Rulesets API only.

**Concurrency policy:** Each entry workflow defines a `concurrency:` group to prevent resource races:

- `ci.yml`: `group: ci::${{ github.ref }}`, `cancel-in-progress: true`
- `buddy.yml`: `group: buddy::${{ github.ref }}::${{ inputs.project-name }}`, `cancel-in-progress: false`
- `official.yml`: `group: official::${{ github.ref }}::${{ inputs.project-name }}`, `cancel-in-progress: false`

The `::` separator is intentional because Git ref names cannot contain `:` under `git check-ref-format`, and valid `project-name` values in this design also exclude `:`; this prevents ambiguous concatenation such as `feat` + `a-b` colliding with `feat-a` + `b`. GitHub Actions still compares concurrency groups case-insensitively, so releasable `project-name` values must also be unique under ASCII lowercase normalization across the repository. With `cancel-in-progress: false`, an in-progress run is preserved. GitHub Actions will replace any existing pending run with the newest queued run for the same concurrency group, so these release concurrency groups are admission locks rather than durable FIFO queues. Queue depth greater than one for the same group is unsupported. Before issuing any fresh dispatch for a concurrency group that already has queued or in-progress runs, operators must inspect the existing runs, then either cancel stale queued runs or wait for the in-progress run to settle rather than assuming the queue will preserve intent. The repository must also run a dedicated release-admission monitor that opens or updates an incident whenever a same-group run is queued behind another live run, or when a queued run in that group disappears or is cancelled without a matching operator-issued cancellation event.

Because workflow-level `concurrency.group` is computed before any job can normalize `github.ref`, this design also forbids mixed-case release workflow source refs. The official protected control-plane branch set is already lowercase-only by construction. Buddy dispatches must likewise use lowercase branch names only; mixed-case buddy source refs are unsupported because case-distinct refs would alias the same concurrency group.

The separator guarantee applies only after `project-name` validation. Because `buddy.yml` and `official.yml` compute their concurrency keys before `resolve-context` runs, an authorized dispatcher can still intentionally collide with another queued run by reusing the same valid `project-name`. Concurrency is therefore an operational coordination control, not a security boundary. A dispatch from a not-yet-eligible branch or otherwise invalid configuration still occupies its concurrency group until the run settles; operators must cancel the known-bad run before redispatching the corrected configuration for the same group. The reviewed dispatcher allowlist described later is therefore a secret-consumption and privileged-progress gate, not a native pre-dispatch admission gate: a non-allowlisted repository writer can still create and transiently occupy an `official.yml` concurrency slot until `authorize-dispatcher` fails. That residual slot-occupation risk is not acceptable silent noise in this design: `.github/workflows/official-run-health-monitor.yml` must detect any same-group `official.yml` run that fails in or immediately after `authorize-dispatcher` with an allowlist-denial outcome, route it as `high-nonpage` immediately, and escalate to `page` if that blocked group also has a queued, requested, waiting, or in-progress allowlisted run for the same `(ref, project-name)` pair or if the occupied slot is not cleared within 15 minutes. Recovery is explicit: cancel the unauthorized run before redispatching the approved release attempt; do not wait for natural completion while the slot is occupied.

For `official.yml`, the concurrency key intentionally serializes per `(ref, project-name)` pair rather than across all protected branches, so it is not sufficient by itself to block same-project official runs from different protected branches such as `main` and `release/<project-name>/v<release-line>`. This design therefore adds a second, repository-wide same-project admission check in `preflight-check`: before any production approval is consumed, that job must enumerate live `official.yml` runs in `queued`, `requested`, `waiting`, or `in_progress` state and hard-fail if another run for the same `project-name` already exists on a different ref. That live-run enumeration is still an advisory lock rather than a transactional security boundary, because GitHub does not document an atomic cross-run reservation primitive for this case. If two same-project cross-ref runs nevertheless overlap because they raced between enumeration and later state transition, that overlap is a control-plane incident rather than tolerated load: no second production approval may be granted until one run is cancelled, and `.github/workflows/official-run-health-monitor.yml` must open or update a `high-nonpage` incident immediately, identify the losing run as the later-created run unless exactly one run has already reached any environment-gated job (in that case the not-yet-environment-gated run loses), and auto-cancel that losing run within 15 minutes whenever it is still `queued`, `requested`, `waiting`, or `in_progress` before `create-release-tag`, `require-provenance`, or any selected publish job. If both overlapping runs have already reached environment-gated jobs or otherwise cannot be ordered by that rule without risking already-mutated release state, the monitor must escalate to `page` immediately rather than waiting for the 15-minute window.

**Job timeouts:** Every job must declare `timeout-minutes`, and workflow linting enforced through `hk`/`actionlint` should fail if any job omits it. Recommended defaults: `preflight-check`, resolution jobs, and static-analysis jobs `15`; Ubuntu build jobs `30`; Windows C# build jobs `45` because hosted Windows runners have materially higher startup and .NET restore/build/test overhead than Ubuntu runners; isolated attestation jobs `15`; `require-provenance` `45` because it now downloads the build artifact plus provenance sidecar artifact, verifies the attestation set, performs bounded evidence-branch append retries with immutable read-back verification, and must emit phase checkpoints for timeout diagnosis; publish jobs `25` except `publish-pypi-official` `35`; `confirm-publish-state` `90` because the same reviewed job must now support both the normal parallel worker model and the approved `serial-degraded` fallback described later in this document, while still covering runner startup, checkout, locked-tool bootstrap, checkpoint persistence, and output serialization. The steady-state expectation remains that a healthy parallel run should finish comfortably inside the first 45 minutes; the 90-minute budget exists so a reviewed serial fallback is possible without a second emergency redesign. Lightweight tag-management jobs `10`; and terminal gate jobs `ci-passed` and `release-complete` `15` because those jobs must perform a read-only checkout, restore the locked tool cache, run `mise install`, and then execute the jq assertions. That 15-minute budget is intentional and does not rely on a perfect warm-cache hit. Some YAML snippets below omit `timeout-minutes` only for brevity; concrete workflow files must still declare it.

**Action pinning:** All external actions, including GitHub-maintained actions under the `actions/` namespace, must be pinned to full commit SHA. Any `docker://` image reference must be pinned to an immutable digest such as `@sha256:...`. Local composite actions under `.github/actions/**` are sourced from the checked-out protected workspace, must be explicitly covered by `CODEOWNERS`, and are governed by the same branch protection and `CODEOWNERS` review as the caller workflow rather than by a separate pin. Use Renovate or Dependabot to manage external action updates:

```yaml
uses: dorny/paths-filter@de90cc6ed7cd597cb74b84a7e832ce805e3c7b15 # v3.0.2
```

The repository's dependency-update automation must cover `.github/workflows/**` so pinned SHAs are refreshed intentionally rather than drifting indefinitely.

Repository policy must run both `actionlint` and `zizmor` in strict mode through `hk`. `actionlint` covers workflow syntax and common semantics. `zizmor` is the authoritative enforcement layer for full-SHA action pinning, digest-pinned `docker://` references, prohibiting `secrets: inherit`, and rejecting `on: pull_request_target`. `on: workflow_run` remains prohibited everywhere except the exact reviewed workflow files `.github/workflows/official-run-health-monitor.yml` and `.github/workflows/control-plane-post-tag-failure.yml`; no other workflow may declare that trigger. The only workflow that may reference any `control-plane-monitoring-<project-name>` environment is `.github/workflows/official.yml`, and only for `preflight-check`. The only workflows that may reference `control-plane-governance-monitoring` are `.github/workflows/control-plane-drift-monitor.yml`, `.github/workflows/nuget-trusted-publisher-readiness.yml`, `.github/workflows/npm-trusted-publisher-readiness.yml`, `.github/workflows/pypi-trusted-publisher-readiness.yml`, `.github/workflows/rubygems-trusted-publisher-readiness.yml`, `.github/workflows/official-run-health-monitor.yml`, `.github/workflows/control-plane-post-tag-failure.yml`, `.github/workflows/open-incident-freshness-monitor.yml`, `.github/workflows/release-operational-audit.yml`, and `.github/workflows/governance-and-runbook-freshness.yml`. Each allowlisted monitoring workflow must hold zero registry credentials, may request no repository write scope beyond the minimum needed for its reviewed alerting or ledger-PR duty, may call the GitHub Releases API only for read-only confirmation and audit queries, must declare an explicit `workflows:` allowlist plus an exact `branches:` filter and a runtime exact-ref check against the caller-ref registry frozen from `main` when it uses `workflow_run`, must self-validate `github.workflow_ref` against its own exact reviewed workflow path before reading any environment secret or minting any GitHub App token, and must not download, execute, or restore artifacts, caches, or code from the triggering run except for the narrow reviewed data-only exceptions in this paragraph. `.github/workflows/control-plane-post-tag-failure.yml` may download only the immutable `tag-reservation-result-<project-name>` artifact from the triggering `official.yml` run as data-only input for recovery correlation; it must not download any other artifact, cache, or code from the triggering run, and it must treat that artifact as untrusted data rather than executable content. `.github/workflows/official-run-health-monitor.yml` is the only monitoring-workflow exception allowed to create or update reviewed ledger-update branches and PRs: it may request only the minimum `contents: write` and `pull-requests: write` scope needed for that reviewed ledger-update path, may download only immutable `candidate-ledger-payload-<project-name>-<run-id>-attempt-<run-attempt>` artifacts as data-only input for that path, and must never use that exception to mutate packages, releases, tags, or any branch other than the reviewed `ledger-update/**` PR branches. Privileged workflows in this design must also reject `issue_comment`, `pull_request_review`, `pull_request_review_comment`, and `pull_request_review_thread` triggers unless a future design adds a dedicated actor-validation model for them. `hk.pkl` must also define the repository-specific policy checks that `actionlint` and `zizmor` do not provide: no reusable-workflow `permissions:` blocks, no unsafe shell sinks or unreviewed workflow-command-file writers in `.github/workflows/**`, `.github/actions/**`, and `eng/scripts/**`, no self-hosted runner labels on any job that requests `id-token: write`, reads any `control-plane-monitoring-*` environment or `control-plane-governance-monitoring`, mutates a registry, mints repository-scoped GitHub App write credentials, mutates protected tags, durable evidence refs, or GitHub Release state, or produces build artifacts for an `official.yml` release, exact `infra` inventory coverage, exact workflow self-checks before any job reads monitoring-environment secrets, hard-fail detection of any `NuGet/login@v1`, `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_*`, or equivalent OIDC-token request path when the frozen `nuget:official` `authMechanism` is `api-key-secret`, hard-fail detection of any `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_*` or equivalent OIDC-token request path anywhere in the selected `publish-rubygems-official-api-key` path when the frozen `rubygems:official` `authMechanism` is `api-key-secret`, and a digest-pinned MISE backend allowlist.

**Tool lock enforcement:** `mise.lock` is required repository state, not optional convenience metadata. `hk check --all` must fail when the repository root lacks `mise.lock`, and any intentional toolchain update must regenerate the lockfile with `mise lock` in the same change that modifies `mise.toml`. Gate jobs that rely on `jq`, including `ci-passed`, `confirm-publish-state`, and both `release-complete` jobs, and provenance jobs that rely on `gh`, including `require-provenance`, must obtain those tools from the repository-managed `mise` toolchain rather than from the runner image, so both `jq` and `gh` are part of the reviewed locked toolchain for this design. Those jobs must therefore perform a read-only checkout, restore a tool cache keyed by `mise.toml` and `mise.lock`, and run `mise install` before the relevant gate step. Zero-permission jq gates are unsupported. The locked `jq` version must be at least `1.6`, and the locked `gh` version must be a reviewed release that exposes the verified JSON fields consumed by Section 8; runner-native `gh` is unsupported for official provenance verification. Because the reviewed `gh attestation verify` docs do not promise a stable failure taxonomy, the repository-reviewed attestation-failure classifier is part of that same locked-tool contract: every intentional `gh` version change must update the classifier fixtures, the recorded reviewed failure-shape expectations, and the self-test evidence in the same change set, and `hk check --all` must reject a `gh` lock update that does not update that coupled classifier-review state. For any project that declares `npm:official`, the same reviewed toolchain state must also pin Node `>= 22.14.0` and npm CLI `>= 11.5.1`; `hk check --all` and `trusted-release-inventory` must hard-fail when the locked toolchain falls below that floor. The reviewed MISE backend policy must also be machine-enforced in `hk.pkl`: only backends whose lockfile entries include immutable upstream digests are allowed in official build or publish paths. Version-string-only backends are unsupported in official build or publish paths. The digest-pinning contract begins only after the `mise` bootstrap itself is trusted. Before any official build, provenance, gate, confirmation, or publish path executes `mise install`, the job must satisfy one of two reviewed bootstrap modes: either verify the `mise` executable against reviewed integrity data (for example an approved SHA-256) or install it from an organization-controlled source with equivalent integrity verification, or explicitly treat the GitHub-hosted runner image as the reviewed trust root for the `mise` executable and bind that assumption to runner-image supply-chain audit and drift-monitoring controls. Running `mise install` on the official path without one of those reviewed bootstrap assurances is unsupported, and `hk.pkl` must fail closed if the selected bootstrap mode is neither verified nor explicitly declared.

## 2. `ci.yml` — PR Validation (Targeted Concurrency, Shift-Left)

**Trigger:** `on: pull_request`

Because `pull_request` runs evaluate the PR merge commit, local workflow files, composite actions, and helper scripts execute from the PR-provided tree. The repository must therefore require explicit approval before workflows from forked pull requests may run. Without that repository setting, `ci-passed` is not a trusted release-gating signal for fork PRs.

For private repositories, this design does not rely on forked `pull_request` workflow execution at all. GitHub does not pass repository or organization secrets to fork-triggered `pull_request` runs, so the metadata-App path used elsewhere in this design is unavailable there. External contributions to a private repository must therefore be mirrored into same-repository branches by a maintainer before this workflow may run.

Because GitHub documents the repository Actions settings needed for fork-PR approval and pull-request write-token policy behind Administration-read APIs, this design does **not** attempt to re-verify those live repository settings from untrusted `pull_request` runs. Those settings are instead repository prerequisites audited by control-plane monitoring from trusted credentials on `main`; `ci.yml` validates checked-in control-plane files and affected test scope only.

CI does not build everything on every PR. It uses path filtering (`dorny/paths-filter`, SHA-pinned) to run only the affected language test suites.

**Jobs:**

1. **`static-analysis`**:
    - `permissions: { contents: read }`
    - Runs `jdx/hk` (`hk check --all`) on an Ubuntu runner. HK auto-detects file types from its configuration (`hk.pkl`), serving as the first gate for formatting and linting failures.
    - The same whole-repo analysis must also enforce the single-language project scope for releasable projects: repository policy must hard-fail if any candidate releasable project root resolves to more than one workflow language.
    - This job is intentionally unconditional whole-repo analysis and must not acquire an `if:` guard without a matching `ci-passed` contract change. If HK wall time ever becomes a material bottleneck, replace it with an explicit path-aware design rather than silently making the job skippable.

2. **`detect-changes`**: Uses `dorny/paths-filter` to classify modified files:
    - `permissions: { pull-requests: read }`
    - `csharp`: `['**/*.cs', '**/*.csproj', '**/*.fsproj', '**/*.vbproj', 'global.json', 'Directory.*.props', 'Directory.Packages.props', 'nuget.config', '**/NuGet.Config', '**/*.targets', '**/packages.lock.json']`
    - `python`: `['**/*.py', 'pyproject.toml', 'uv.lock']`
    - `jsts`: `['**/*.ts', '**/*.js', '**/*.mjs', '**/*.cjs', 'package.json', 'pnpm-workspace.yaml', 'pnpm-lock.yaml', 'biome.jsonc', 'tsconfig*.json']`
    - `ruby`: `['**/*.rb', '**/*.gemspec', '**/Gemfile', '**/Gemfile.lock']`
    - `infra`: `['.github/workflows/**', '.github/actions/**', '.github/CODEOWNERS', '.github/official-caller-refs.json', '.github/official-dispatch-authorizers.json', '.github/publish-trust-inventory.json', '.github/provenance-signer-map.json', '.github/release-recovery-ledger.jsonl', '.github/release-recovery-ledger-archive-*.jsonl', 'eng/scripts/**', '**/release.json', '**/version.json', 'mise.toml', 'mise.lock', 'hk.pkl', 'PklProject', 'PklProject.deps.json']`

    When `infra` changes are detected, all language test suites are triggered regardless of other filters.

    The `infra` filter is the authoritative CI-maintained inventory of trust-bearing **cross-language** control-plane files for release validation. Ecosystem-local dependency-control files, even when they live at repository root, must stay only in their language-specific filters so C#-, Python-, JavaScript/TypeScript-, and Ruby-specific toolchain changes do not spuriously trigger the other ecosystems' whole-language suites. In particular, the C#-ecosystem-local files already listed under `csharp` — `global.json`, `Directory.*.props`, `Directory.Packages.props`, `nuget.config`, `**/NuGet.Config`, `**/*.targets`, and `**/packages.lock.json` — must remain excluded from `infra` and must not be duplicated there. Any reviewed change that adds, removes, or renames trusted helper code or shared cross-language control-plane files consumed by official build or release jobs must update this filter in the same PR; there is no separate compatibility fallback to a broader implicit catch-all.

    Repository policy must machine-enforce that invariant rather than relying on reviewer memory alone. In addition to `dorny/paths-filter`, `hk check --all` must run a control-plane inventory check that recomputes the expected `infra` filter members from the trusted **cross-language** file classes in this design and hard-fails on any missing entry, stale entry, or trusted cross-language file change that would not set `infra = true`.

    > **Scaling note:** The current filters operate at language level (`**/*.cs` triggers all C# builds). As the monorepo grows past ~10 projects per language, this should evolve to per-project granularity using affected-project detection from `eng/scripts/find_project_path.py`.

3. **`trusted-release-inventory`**:
    - `needs: [detect-changes]`
    - `permissions: { contents: read }`
    - Conditional: `if: needs.detect-changes.outputs.infra == 'true'`
    - Checks out the PR merge commit as data-only input under `path: .candidate-pr` and also checks out `refs/heads/main` as the trusted validator source under `path: .ctrl-main`, both with `persist-credentials: false`, and runs the repository-side drift check for `.github/publish-trust-inventory.json`. Any helper script, schema validator, or jq/Python logic executed by this job must come only from `.ctrl-main/`; `.candidate-pr/` provides the candidate post-change control-plane data being validated and must remain data-only. This job must recompute the expected post-change trust-bearing state from the PR checkout's candidate control-plane files and validated `release.json` files, using the trusted validator logic from `.ctrl-main/` and deriving each project's exact `allowedCallerRefs` from the candidate `.github/official-caller-refs.json` as `refs/heads/main` plus only those maintenance refs that exactly match `refs/heads/release/<project-name>/v<major>.<minor>.x`. It must compare the exact normalized values of `schemaVersion`, `entryWorkflowPath`, and the per-project `language`, `currentMainReleaseLine`, derived `allowedCallerRefs`, `targets[*].publishExecutionPath`, `targets[*].environment`, `targets[*].authMechanism`, optional `targets[*].trustedPublisherSelector`, optional `targets[*].documentedOidcAudience`, optional `targets[*].oidcAudienceEndpoint`, optional `targets[*].providerContractStatus`, optional `targets[*].providerContractObservedAt`, and optional `targets[*].providerContractExpiresAt` fields. The same job must also cross-validate that every trust-bearing target declared in each releasable project's candidate `release.json` has exactly one matching inventory target entry and that the candidate inventory does not contain any orphan trust-bearing target absent from the project's validated candidate `release.json`. In this inventory, the trust-bearing target set is every official target plus `pypi:testpypi`; buddy GitHub Packages targets remain excluded because they use only `GITHUB_TOKEN` and do not rely on external registry-side trusted-publisher selectors or OIDC-audience discovery. When a candidate change modifies any project's `currentMainReleaseLine` or project-scoped `allowedCallerRefs` relative to the authoritative `main` baseline, the same PR must also add or update one reviewed `audit` ledger record with `scope = "project-release-line"` whose `evidenceUrl` proves the corresponding branch creation/protection, retirement cleanup, or transition hold record for that exact release-line change; missing same-change transition evidence is a hard failure. When any releasable project declares `npm:official`, the same job must also assert from the candidate locked toolchain state that Node `>= 22.14.0` and npm CLI `>= 11.5.1` are satisfied for that production path. Any missing inventory update, stale mapping, malformed schema, mismatched current-main-release-line, mismatched environment mapping, mismatched auth mechanism, mismatched trusted-publisher selector, mismatched fixed-audience mapping, mismatched audience-discovery-endpoint mapping, mismatched provider-contract-status mapping, mismatched provider-contract-gap timing fields, missing same-change release-line transition evidence, release-config mismatch, locked-toolchain floor violation for `npm:official`, or `schemaVersion != 5` is a hard failure.
    - The same job must also validate `.github/CODEOWNERS` whenever that file or any trust-bearing inventory file changes. Validation must prove that every trust-bearing path class named in this design remains covered by the dedicated release-engineering owners and that those patterns still cover `.github/workflows/**`, `.github/actions/**`, the checked-in trust inventories, and every reviewed helper path consumed by official release control-plane code.
    - The same job must also validate `.github/official-dispatch-authorizers.json` whenever that file changes, including `schemaVersion`, the strict top-level key whitelist, exact-login string normalization rules for `users`, exact decimal-string normalization rules for `appIds` as GitHub **account IDs** rather than GitHub App identifiers, exact object-key normalization and coverage rules for `appIdBindings`, uniqueness within each actor class, and the requirement that at least one actor entry exists across `{users, appIds}`. `appIds` stores the bot-user numeric ID that GitHub surfaces at runtime as `github.actor_id` for an app-triggered run, not the GitHub App ID shown on the app settings page. Any reviewed GitHub App bot identity approved by this file is dual-registered by design: its bot login must appear in `users` for rerun admission, its bot-user account ID must appear in `appIds` for app-triggered initial-run admission, and `appIdBindings` must carry the same reviewed binding keyed by that exact account ID. CI must reject one-sided bot registration in either direction and must reject any `appIdBindings` object whose keys are not an exact one-to-one match for `appIds`. Each `appIdBindings[<account-id>]` value must be an object with exactly `login` and `evidence` string fields, where `login` matches one entry in `users` exactly and `evidence` is a non-empty reviewed evidence reference or note derived from the bot lookup path such as `GET /users/<app-slug>[bot]` and its returned `id`. Numeric plausibility heuristics may be used as an additional sanity check, but they are not sufficient and must never replace this same-file evidence-backed validation.
    - The same job must also validate `.github/provenance-signer-map.json` against the Section 6 Verifier signer mapping contract schema whenever that file changes, including `schemaVersion`, the exact top-level keys, the closed language set, one required fully qualified `jobWorkflowRefTemplate` for each language entry, one exact attestation-job mapping for each enabled official language, and the physical presence of the declared attestation workflow file in the candidate tree. The validator must also require exactly one literal `{ref}` placeholder in each `jobWorkflowRefTemplate`, reject templates that pre-expand, omit, or repeat that placeholder, require the repository-relative workflow path embedded in `jobWorkflowRefTemplate` to equal the sibling `workflowPath` exactly, and hard-fail if `.candidate-pr/<workflowPath>` does not exist as a regular file. `attestationJob` is routing and audit state, while `jobWorkflowRefTemplate` is the verifier-facing signer template later bound to the trusted runtime caller ref from `official.yml`, not to any build-supplied or post-verification-derived string.
    - The same job must also validate the active recovery ledger `.github/release-recovery-ledger.jsonl` plus any `.github/release-recovery-ledger-archive-*.jsonl` segments against the Section 7 schema whenever any of those files change, using the reviewed repository helper under `.ctrl-main/eng/scripts/**` as the authoritative semantic validator. That validator must load the entire active JSONL stream rather than validating active-file lines in isolation, must validate each archive file as a standalone complete segment, must enforce the active/archive split and size-budget rules defined in Section 7, and must reject any `incidentId` or `auditId` whose revision chain is split across files or appears non-contiguously within a file. That validator must enforce `schemaVersion`, strict key whitelists, `incidentId` UUID requirements, required `revision` monotonicity per `incidentId`, `auditId` UUID requirements, required `revision` monotonicity per `auditId`, required `releaseLine`, required `evidenceUrl`, the required incident and audit governance fields (`owner`, `severity`, `acknowledgedAt`, and `nextReviewAt` where applicable), closed sets, conditional `runAttempt`, `workflowRunUrl`, `artifactEvidenceUrl`, `closedAt`, `automationId`, `scriptVersion`, and `credentialId` rules, canonical target ordering, the `selectedTargets` / `publishedTargets` / `unpublishedTargets` partition invariants, the `deprecatedTargets`, `delistedTargets`, `removedTargets`, and `retainedTargets` subset invariants, the disposition-specific distinguishing rules for `open-before-publish`, `open-partial-publish`, `recovered`, `abandoned-before-publish`, `abandoned-after-partial-publish`, `burned`, `partially-withdrawn`, and `fully-withdrawn`, exhaustive target accounting for terminal published states, the hard-failure rule that every `delistedTargets` entry must belong to the reviewed `delist-capable` target set defined in Section 7, and the presence-and-absence rules for the hold-window evidence fields used in destructive stable-release recovery.
    - The same job must also diff each candidate `release.json` against the authoritative `main` baseline. If a candidate PR removes any official target for a project and the authoritative ledger history on `main` shows that target was previously published for that project, the same PR must also update `.github/release-recovery-ledger.jsonl` to classify the surviving state for that target under `deprecatedTargets`, `delistedTargets`, `removedTargets`, or `retainedTargets` as applicable. Omitting that ledger update is a hard failure.

4. **`test-csharp` / `test-python` / `test-jsts` / `test-ruby`** (run in parallel):
    - `needs: [detect-changes, static-analysis]`
    - `permissions: { contents: read }`
    - Conditional: e.g. `if: needs.detect-changes.outputs.csharp == 'true' || needs.detect-changes.outputs.infra == 'true'`
    - Each calls its corresponding reusable workflow in `build-scope: ci` mode. In this mode the caller omits `project-path` and `project-name`, the reusable workflow executes the language-wide CI suite for the current checkout, and `require-provenance` must remain `false`. C# uses `windows-latest`; the others use `ubuntu-latest`.

5. **`ci-passed`** (final gate job):
    - `if: always()`
    - `permissions: { contents: read }`
    - `needs: [detect-changes, static-analysis, trusted-release-inventory, test-csharp, test-python, test-jsts, test-ruby]`
    - Before the jq assertion runs, this job must check out the repository read-only with `persist-credentials: false`, restore the `mise` tool cache keyed by `mise.toml` plus `mise.lock`, and run `mise install` so the jq gate uses the reviewed locked toolchain rather than the runner image.
    - Asserts all required checks either passed or were legitimately skipped. Including `detect-changes`, `static-analysis`, and `trusted-release-inventory` in `needs` ensures their failures block the gate — if `detect-changes` fails, all downstream conditional jobs are auto-skipped with `result: "skipped"`, and without `detect-changes` in `needs`, `ci-passed` would see only `"success"` and `"skipped"` results and falsely pass. The gate must also re-derive which language suites were required from `detect-changes.outputs` so a drifted `if:` condition on a `test-*` job cannot silently convert a required suite into a tolerated skip, and it must hard-fail if any expected `detect-changes` output key is missing or not one of `"true"` / `"false"`.
    - `detect-changes` and `static-analysis` are intentionally unconditional. Neither may acquire an `if:` guard without a matching `ci-passed` contract change.
    - The normative jq skeleton is logical rather than a literal requirement to pass the entire `needs` object through one environment variable. Implementations must project `needs` down to the compact set of fields the gate actually consumes before handing JSON to `jq`, so runner environment-size limits cannot silently become a correctness bug in larger monorepos.

    Illustrative fragment only; this block is a workflow logic sketch, not standalone valid YAML.

    ```text
    ci-passed:
        if: always()
        permissions:
            contents: read
        needs: [detect-changes, static-analysis, trusted-release-inventory, test-csharp, test-python, test-jsts, test-ruby]
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
            - id: collect-gate-input
              name: Collect compact gate input
              uses: ./.github/actions/collect-gate-input
              with:
                  jobs-json: ${{ toJson(needs) }}
                  include-jobs: detect-changes,static-analysis,trusted-release-inventory,test-csharp,test-python,test-jsts,test-ruby
            - name: Assert all required checks passed or were legitimately skipped
              env:
                  GATE_INPUT_JSON: ${{ steps.collect-gate-input.outputs.gate-input-json }}
              run: |
                  jq -n -e '
                      (env.GATE_INPUT_JSON | fromjson) as $n
                      | ($n["detect-changes"].outputs) as $dc
                      | ($n["detect-changes"].result == "success")
                      and ($n["static-analysis"].result == "success")
                      and (["csharp", "python", "jsts", "ruby", "infra"]
                          | all(. as $key | ($dc[$key] == "true" or $dc[$key] == "false")))
                      and (if ($dc.infra == "true")
                          then $n["trusted-release-inventory"].result == "success"
                          else $n["trusted-release-inventory"].result == "skipped"
                          end)
                      and (if ($dc.csharp == "true" or $dc.infra == "true")
                          then $n["test-csharp"].result == "success"
                          else $n["test-csharp"].result == "skipped"
                          end)
                      and (if ($dc.python == "true" or $dc.infra == "true")
                          then $n["test-python"].result == "success"
                          else $n["test-python"].result == "skipped"
                          end)
                      and (if ($dc.jsts == "true" or $dc.infra == "true")
                          then $n["test-jsts"].result == "success"
                          else $n["test-jsts"].result == "skipped"
                          end)
                      and (if ($dc.ruby == "true" or $dc.infra == "true")
                          then $n["test-ruby"].result == "success"
                          else $n["test-ruby"].result == "skipped"
                          end)'
    ```

## 3. `buddy.yml` — Unofficial Release (Static Conditional Publish)

**Trigger:** `on: workflow_dispatch` only (no automated triggers).

**Inputs:**

| Input          | Type      | Required | Description                 |
| -------------- | --------- | -------- | --------------------------- |
| `project-name` | `string`  | Yes      | Project identity to release |

All workflow inputs must be mapped to intermediate environment variables before use in shell scripts (e.g., `env: PROJECT_NAME: ${{ inputs.project-name }}`; use `"$PROJECT_NAME"` in bash, never `${{ inputs.project-name }}` directly in `run:` blocks).

Same-repository `pull_request` runs from collaborators with repository write access remain inside the trusted-collaborator boundary for read-only CI only. Those runs must never mint production OIDC credentials, must never enter any `production-*` environment, and must never receive GitHub App write tokens.

Buddy is intentionally allowed to release from development branches. It does **not** require ancestry to `main` or to a maintenance release branch.

Even within the same language, different projects may have different packaging strategies (EXE, NuGet, wheel, etc.). The workflow resolves publish targets dynamically from project configuration.

**Jobs:**

1. **`resolve-context`**:
    - `permissions: { contents: read }`
    - **Runner and tooling:** Runs on `ubuntu-latest`. Requires `mise install` to bootstrap Python (for `eng/scripts/find_project_path.py`) and the .NET SDK. The `nbgv-python` adapter is sourced from the current checked-out repository workspace, not from an external package index, so trusted version resolution tracks the selected source ref rather than an out-of-band registry artifact. The `mise.toml` and `mise.lock` at the repo root pin tool versions and, where supported by the selected MISE backends, the exact download digests. Every tool used in an official build or publish path must use a digest-pinning backend; version-string-only backends are unsupported in this design. The job must hard-fail if `mise.lock` is absent, and should restore a tool cache keyed by both files before invoking `mise install`.
    - **Input validation:** As the first step (before any checkout or git operation), validate `project-name` with a full-string match against the character class `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]*`, require length `1..100`, reject any occurrence of the substring `..`, reject trailing `.`, and reject any name that ends with `.lock`. Reject invalid names with a clear error. Releasable project identities in this design are ASCII-lowercase only so branch names, environment names, tag names, and concurrency keys all use one canonical spelling.
    - **Source ref policy:** Buddy intentionally permits dispatch from non-default branches, but only branch refs are supported. `workflow_dispatch` requests that name a tag or any other non-branch ref are hard failures before checkout. No ancestry check against `main` or any release branch is performed in this workflow.
    - Runs `eng/scripts/find_project_path.py` to determine the project path and the workflow language. `project-name` is ASCII-lowercase and must resolve to exactly one releasable project in the repository whose leaf directory name uses that same canonical lowercase spelling. The resolution step must emit exactly one of `{csharp, python, jsts, ruby}` for `language`; no match, ambiguous match, unsupported language, or resolver error is a hard failure.
    - **NBGV resolution:** The checkout must use `fetch-depth: 0` so NBGV can compute version height from git history. Read-only checkouts in this job must also use `persist-credentials: false`. All jobs that use NBGV or rely on git-history-derived metadata must also checkout with full history. The script locates the correct `version.json` by searching upward from the project directory. In this design, inheriting the nearest ancestor `version.json` when the project root does not have its own local file is intentional, but the governing file must still resolve uniquely. "Resolve deterministically" therefore means: on a full-history checkout of the selected ref, `nbgv-python` finds exactly one governing `version.json`, emits exactly one normalized version string, and that string passes the language-specific validator.
